title: Ἡ εἰς Ἀίδαο ὁδός
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, won over by his men, asks Circe to keep her promise to send them home. She tells him that first he must make another journey, to the house of Hades, to consult the soul of the blind Theban seer Tiresias. He weeps on her bed until he has no more tears, then asks who will guide a ship to Hades. Circe says that the North Wind will carry the ship across Oceanus, and she lays out in detail where to land, how to dig the pit, which offerings to pour and which animals to sacrifice, and how to keep the dead from the blood until Tiresias has come. At dawn she dresses him, and he rouses his men. One of them, the youngest, Elpenor, who had gone to sleep drunk on the roof, wakes in confusion, falls from it and breaks his neck. Odysseus tells the rest of the new journey, and they weep. At the shore they find that Circe has passed them unseen and tied up a ram and a black ewe by the ship.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαν, αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephan, autar emoi g’ epepeitheto thymos agēnōr.
sentences.l: So they spoke, and my own manly spirit was persuaded.
sentences.i: So they spoke, and my own proud spirit was won over.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαν is ‘so they spoke’: ἔφαν is the third plural imperfect of φημί ‘say’ (Attic ἔφασαν), the crew's reply that closed the last part. ἐπεπείθετο is the imperfect middle of πείθω ‘persuade’, which in the middle means ‘be persuaded, yield’. ἐμοί γε is ‘in my case’, the dative of the person. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is a stock phrase, ‘manly spirit’ in the Greek-order line and ‘proud spirit’ in the prose: ἀγήνωρ is built on ἀνήρ ‘man’, and θυμός here is the spirit that decides.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε μὲν πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
ἥμεθα, δαινύμενοι κρέα τ’ ἄσπετα καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
sentences.tr:
hōs tote men propan ēmar es ēelion katadynta
hēmetha, dainymenoi krea t’ aspeta kai methy hēdy·
sentences.l:
So then for the whole day, until the sun going down,
we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.i: So for that whole day, until the sun went down, we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.n: πρόπαν ἦμαρ is ‘the whole day’, an accusative of duration, and ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα is ‘until the sun going down’ (ἠέλιον is Attic ἥλιον, with the aorist participle of καταδύω ‘sink’). ἥμεθα is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’ and δαινύμενοι is ‘feasting’. κρέα ἄσπετα is ‘boundless meat’: ἄσπετος is literally ‘not to be told’, and μέθυ ἡδύ is ‘sweet wine’. The two lines are a formula that has already been shipped, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος κατέδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθεν,
οἱ μὲν κοιμήσαντο κατὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ēelios katedy kai epi knephas ēlthen,
hoi men koimēsanto kata megara skioenta.
sentences.l:
And when the sun set and darkness came on,
they, for their part, lay down to sleep through the shadowy halls.
sentences.i: And when the sun set and darkness came on, they lay down to sleep through the shadowy halls.
sentences.n: ἦμος is ‘when’, a Homeric time-word (Attic ὅτε), and κατέδυ is the aorist of καταδύω ‘sink’. ἐπὶ … ἦλθεν is tmesis: the preverb stands apart from ἦλθεν, so ‘darkness came on’ (κνέφας ‘darkness’). The first line is the formula of 9.168, and its English is kept. οἱ μέν is ‘they, for their part’, the pronoun use of the article, set against αὐτὰρ ἐγώ in the next line. κοιμήσαντο is the aorist middle of κοιμάω ‘put to sleep’, and μέγαρα σκιόεντα ‘shadowy halls’ has an adjective from σκιά ‘shadow’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ Κίρκης ἐπιβὰς περικαλλέος εὐνῆς
γούνων ἐλλιτάνευσα, θεὰ δέ μευ ἔκλυεν αὐδῆς·
sentences.tr:
autar egō Kirkēs epibas perikalleos eunēs
gounōn ellitaneusa, thea de meu eklyen audēs·
sentences.l:
But I, having set foot upon Circe’s very fair bed,
entreated her at the knees, and the goddess heard my voice;
sentences.i: But I mounted Circe’s very fair bed and entreated her at her knees, and the goddess heard my voice;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐγώ turns from the sleeping men to Odysseus. ἐπιβάς, the aorist participle of ἐπιβαίνω ‘step upon’, takes the genitive Κίρκης … εὐνῆς, ‘Circe's bed’, and περικαλλέος is ‘very fair’ (περι- is intensive). γούνων ἐλλιτάνευσα is ‘I entreated her at her knees’, the suppliant's posture, with the aorist of λιτανεύω. θεὰ δέ μευ ἔκλυεν αὐδῆς is ‘and the goddess heard my voice’: μευ is epic μου, and κλύω takes the genitive.

sentences.t: καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων·
sentences.tr: kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēudōn·
sentences.l: and speaking to her, winged words I addressed to her:
sentences.i: and I spoke to her and addressed her with winged words:
sentences.n: καί μιν φωνήσας … προσηύδων is the first-person form of a formula: φωνήσας is the aorist participle of φωνέω ‘speak’, μιν ‘her’ (the pronoun has all three genders), and προσηύδων the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ are words that fly from speaker to hearer. The raised point leads into Odysseus' request, and the English of this line follows the wording already shipped.

sentences.t:
ὢ Κίρκη, τέλεσόν μοι ὑπόσχεσιν ἥν περ ὑπέστης,
οἴκαδε πεμψέμεναι· θυμὸς δέ μοι ἔσσυται ἤδη,
sentences.tr:
ō Kirkē, teleson moi hyposchesin hēn per hypestēs,
oikade pempsemenai· thymos de moi essytai ēdē,
sentences.l:
‘O Circe, fulfil for me the promise which you promised,
homeward to send me; and my heart is hastening already,
sentences.i: ‘Circe, fulfil the promise you made me, to send me home; and my heart is already in haste,
sentences.n: The Greek prints no quotation marks. ὢ Κίρκη is ‘O Circe’. τέλεσον is the aorist imperative of τελέω ‘fulfil’, and ὑπόσχεσιν ἥν περ ὑπέστης is ‘the promise which you undertook’ (ὑπέστης is the aorist of ὑφίστημι ‘undertake, promise’). πεμψέμεναι is an epic future infinitive in -έμεναι (Attic πέμψειν), ‘to send’, with οἴκαδε ‘homeward’. ἔσσυται is the perfect passive of σεύω ‘set in motion’, so ‘my heart has been set hurrying’; θυμός is plain ‘heart’ here.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ἄλλων ἑτάρων, οἵ μευ φθινύθουσι φίλον κῆρ
ἀμφ’ ἔμ’ ὀδυρόμενοι, ὅτε που σύ γε νόσφι γένηαι.
sentences.tr:
ēd’ allōn hetarōn, hoi meu phthinythousi philon kēr
amph’ em’ odyromenoi, hote pou sy ge nosphi genēai.
sentences.l:
and that of my other companions, who waste away my dear heart
around me lamenting, whenever you chance to be away.’
sentences.i: and that of my other companions, who wear away the heart in my breast with their weeping around me whenever you are away.’
sentences.n: ἠδ’ ἄλλων ἑτάρων is ‘and (the hearts) of my other companions’: the genitive hangs on the θυμός of the line before. οἵ μευ φθινύθουσι φίλον κῆρ is ‘who waste away my dear heart’; φθινύθω is an epic by-form of φθίνω, here transitive, and μευ is ‘my’. ἀμφ’ ἔμ’ ὀδυρόμενοι is ‘lamenting around me’. ὅτε που σύ γε νόσφι γένηαι is ‘whenever you happen to be away’: γένηαι is the uncontracted aorist subjunctive. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hē d’ autik’ ameibeto dia theaōn·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and she at once answered, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: So I said, and she, heavenly even among goddesses, answered at once:
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I said’, the imperfect middle of φημί. ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, the article used as a pronoun. ἀμείβετο is ‘answered’ with no augment, and αὐτίκα is ‘at once’. δῖα θεάων, ‘heavenly even among goddesses’, is the stock epithet for Circe: θεάων is the genitive plural of θεά, with the epic ending -άων. The whole line has already been shipped and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
μηκέτι νῦν ἀέκοντες ἐμῷ ἐνὶ μίμνετε οἴκῳ.
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē, polymēchan’ Odysseu,
mēketi nyn aekontes emōi eni mimnete oikōi.
sentences.l:
‘Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
no longer now remain unwilling in my house.
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, do not stay on any longer in my house against your will.
sentences.n: διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ is the full vocative (Λαερτιάδη, the patronymic from Λαέρτης, and πολυμήχαν’ for πολυμήχανε). ἀέκοντες is ‘unwilling’ (ἀ- + ἑκών), and the plural shows that she speaks to Odysseus and his men together; μίμνετε is the plural imperative of μίμνω ‘stay’, and μηκέτι νῦν ‘no longer now’ makes it a prohibition. ἐμῷ ἐνὶ … οἴκῳ is ‘in my house’, with ἐνί for ἐν.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄλλην χρὴ πρῶτον ὁδὸν τελέσαι καὶ ἱκέσθαι
εἰς Ἀίδαο δόμους καὶ ἐπαινῆς Περσεφονείης,
ψυχῇ χρησομένους Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο,
μάντηος ἀλαοῦ, τοῦ τε φρένες ἔμπεδοί εἰσι·
sentences.tr:
all’ allēn chrē prōton hodon telesai kai hikesthai
eis Aidao domous kai epainēs Persephoneiēs,
psychēi chrēsomenous Thēbaiou Teiresiao,
mantēos alaou, tou te phrenes empedoi eisi·
sentences.l:
But another journey first you must complete and reach,
to the halls of Hades and of grim Persephone,
to consult the soul of Theban Tiresias,
the blind seer, whose wits are firm;
sentences.i: But first you must complete another journey and come to the halls of Hades and grim Persephone, to consult the soul of Theban Tiresias, the blind seer, whose wits are firm;
sentences.n: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the infinitives τελέσαι ‘complete’ and ἱκέσθαι ‘reach’. Ἀίδαο is the epic genitive of Ἀΐδης, so εἰς Ἀίδαο δόμους is ‘to the halls of Hades’. ἐπαινῆς, the epithet of Persephone, is rendered ‘grim’: it is traditionally taken as ‘dread, awful’, but its exact sense is not certain (it comes again at 534 and 564). ψυχῇ χρησομένους is ‘to consult the soul’: χράομαι takes the dative, and the future participle gives purpose. Τειρεσίαο is Τειρεσίου, and μάντηος is μάντεως, ‘of the seer’. ἀλαοῦ is ‘blind’, and ἔμπεδοί is ‘firm’. Lines 491–492 return at 564–565. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the final short syllable of μάντηος is treated as long at the start of the second foot, before ἀλαοῦ.

sentences.t:
τῷ καὶ τεθνηῶτι νόον πόρε Περσεφόνεια,
οἴῳ πεπνῦσθαι, τοὶ δὲ σκιαὶ ἀίσσουσιν.
sentences.tr:
tōi kai tethnēōti noon pore Persephoneia,
oiōi pepnysthai, toi de skiai aissousin.
sentences.l:
to him, even dead, a mind gave Persephone,
alone to have understanding, but the others flit as shadows.’
sentences.i: Even in death Persephone gave him a mind, so that he alone has understanding, while the rest flit about as shadows.’
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘to him’ (the article as a pronoun), and τεθνηῶτι is the uncontracted epic dative of the perfect participle of θνῄσκω ‘die’, so ‘though dead’. νόον πόρε is ‘gave a mind’: πόρε is an unaugmented aorist of πόρω ‘give’, and νόον is νοῦν. οἴῳ πεπνῦσθαι is ‘alone to have understanding’, the perfect infinitive of πέπνυμαι ‘be wise’, whose participle is πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’. τοὶ δέ is ‘but they’, and ἀίσσουσιν is ‘they dart, flit’. Circe's speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γε κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar emoi ge kateklasthē philon ētor·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and my own heart was broken within me;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and my heart was broken within me;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so she spoke’ (ἔφατο, elided). αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γε is ‘but for me, in my case’. κατεκλάσθη is the aorist passive of κατακλάω ‘break down’, said of the heart, and φίλον ἦτορ ‘my dear heart’ has ἦτορ for the heart as the seat of feeling. The same phrase is used at 566 of the men, with the persons changed.

sentences.t:
κλαῖον δ’ ἐν λεχέεσσι καθήμενος, οὐδέ νύ μοι κῆρ
ἤθελ’ ἔτι ζώειν καὶ ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.tr:
klaion d’ en lecheessi kathēmenos, oude ny moi kēr
ēthel’ eti zōein kai horan phaos ēelioio.
sentences.l:
and I wept, sitting on the bed, nor at all did my heart
wish still to live and to look upon the light of the sun.
sentences.i: and I sat weeping on the bed, and I no longer wished to go on living and to see the light of the sun.
sentences.n: κλαῖον is the imperfect ‘I wept’, with no augment. ἐν λεχέεσσι is ‘on the bed’: λέχεα is a plural for one bed, with the epic dative ending -εσσι. οὐδέ νύ μοι κῆρ ἤθελ’ is ‘nor did my heart any longer wish’; ἤθελε is the imperfect of ἐθέλω. ζώειν is the uncontracted infinitive (Attic ζῆν), and ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο ‘to look upon the light of the sun’ is the phrase for being alive; ἠελίοιο is the epic genitive in -οιο for -ου.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κλαίων τε κυλινδόμενος τ’ ἐκορέσθην,
καὶ τότε δή μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr:
autar epei klaiōn te kylindomenos t’ ekoresthēn,
kai tote dē min epessin ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l:
But when I had had my fill of weeping and of rolling about,
then indeed with words, answering her, I addressed her:
sentences.i: But when I had had my fill of weeping and of rolling about, then I answered her, and spoke:
sentences.n: ἐκορέσθην is the aorist passive of κορέννυμι ‘satisfy’, so ‘I had had my fill’, with the participles κλαίων … κυλινδόμενος ‘of weeping and of rolling about’ (κυλίνδομαι ‘roll’). καὶ τότε δή is ‘and then at last’. μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is ‘answering her with words, I addressed her’: ἔπεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ἔπος, and προσέειπον is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’.

sentences.t: ὢ Κίρκη, τίς γὰρ ταύτην ὁδὸν ἡγεμονεύσει;
sentences.tr: ō Kirkē, tis gar tautēn hodon hēgemoneusei;
sentences.l: ‘O Circe, for who will guide this journey?
sentences.i: ‘Circe, who, then, will guide us on this journey?
sentences.n: ὢ Κίρκη, τίς γάρ … is ‘O Circe, for who …’: γάρ gives the ground of the question, and the Greek question mark ends the unit. ἡγεμονεύσει is the future of ἡγεμονεύω ‘lead the way’, and ταύτην ὁδόν is the accusative of the road travelled, ‘on this journey’.

sentences.t: εἰς Ἄϊδος δ’ οὔ πώ τις ἀφίκετο νηὶ μελαίνῃ.
sentences.tr: eis Aïdos d’ ou pō tis aphiketo nēi melainēi.
sentences.l: and to Hades no one has yet come in a black ship.’
sentences.i: No one has yet gone to Hades in a black ship.’
sentences.n: εἰς Ἄϊδος δ’ is ‘and to Hades’: the genitive Ἄϊδος has a word like ‘house’ understood, as in Ἀίδαο δόμους at 491. οὔ πώ τις ἀφίκετο is ‘no one has yet arrived’. νηὶ μελαίνῃ is ‘in a black ship’, the epic dative of νηῦς with its stock epithet. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hē d’ autik’ ameibeto dia theaōn·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and she at once answered, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: So I said, and she, heavenly even among goddesses, answered at once:
sentences.n: The same line as 487, with the same English. ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, ἀμείβετο ‘answered’, and δῖα θεάων is Circe's stock epithet, ‘heavenly even among goddesses’, with the genitive plural θεάων.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
μή τί τοι ἡγεμόνος γε ποθὴ παρὰ νηὶ μελέσθω,
ἱστὸν δὲ στήσας, ἀνά θ’ ἱστία λευκὰ πετάσσας
ἧσθαι·
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē, polymēchan’ Odysseu,
mē ti toi hēgemonos ge pothē para nēi melesthō,
histon de stēsas, ana th’ histia leuka petassas
hēsthai·
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, let no want of a guide trouble you by the ship, but set up the mast, spread the white sails, and sit;
sentences.n: Line 504 is the vocative of 488, with its English. μή τί τοι … μελέσθω is ‘let nothing be a care to you’: μελέσθω is the third-person imperative of μέλομαι, τοι is ‘to you’, and ποθή ‘longing, want’ takes the genitive ἡγεμόνος ‘for a guide’. ἱστὸν … στήσας and ἀνά … πετάσσας (tmesis) are aorist participles, ‘having set up the mast, having spread the sails’; ἧσθαι ‘to sit’ is an infinitive for an imperative. ἱστία λευκά is ‘white sails’.

sentences.t: τὴν δέ κέ τοι πνοιὴ Βορέαο φέρῃσιν.
sentences.tr: tēn de ke toi pnoiē Boreao pherēisin.
sentences.l: and her the breath of the North Wind will carry for you.
sentences.i: and the breath of the North Wind will carry the ship for you.
sentences.n: τήν is ‘her’, the ship, feminine as νηῦς is. κε with the subjunctive φέρῃσιν gives the future sense ‘will carry’; τοι is ‘for you’. πνοιή is ‘breath, blowing’, and Βορέαο is the epic genitive of Βορέης, ‘the North Wind’. The unit starts in the middle of line 507, after the raised point.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν δὴ νηὶ δι’ Ὠκεανοῖο περήσῃς,
ἔνθ’ ἀκτή τε λάχεια καὶ ἄλσεα Περσεφονείης,
μακραί τ’ αἴγειροι καὶ ἰτέαι ὠλεσίκαρποι,
sentences.tr:
all’ hopot’ an dē nēi di’ Ōkeanoio perēsēis,
enth’ aktē te lacheia kai alsea Persephoneiēs,
makrai t’ aigeiroi kai iteai ōlesikarpoi,
sentences.l:
But when, then, in your ship across Oceanus you have crossed,
there where is a low-lying shore and the groves of Persephone,
both tall poplars and willows that lose their fruit,
sentences.i: But when you have crossed Oceanus in your ship, to where there is a low-lying shore and the groves of Persephone, tall poplars and willows that lose their fruit,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν δὴ … περήσῃς is ‘but when you have crossed’, with the aorist subjunctive; Ὠκεανοῖο is the epic genitive of Ὠκεανός. ἔνθ’ is ‘where’. ἀκτὴ λάχεια is ‘a low-lying shore’; the meaning of λάχεια is not certain, and ‘low-lying’ is the traditional guess. ἄλσεα is the uncontracted ‘groves’. αἴγειροι are ‘black poplars’ and ἰτέαι ‘willows’. ὠλεσίκαρποι is ‘fruit-losing’ (ὄλλυμι ‘destroy, lose’ + καρπός). The long sentence is cut at this comma.

sentences.t:
νῆα μὲν αὐτοῦ κέλσαι ἐπ’ Ὠκεανῷ βαθυδίνῃ,
αὐτὸς δ’ εἰς Ἀίδεω ἰέναι δόμον εὐρώεντα.
sentences.tr:
nēa men autou kelsai ep’ Ōkeanōi bathydinēi,
autos d’ eis Aideō ienai domon eurōenta.
sentences.l:
beach the ship right there, at deep-eddying Oceanus,
and go yourself to the mouldy house of Hades.
sentences.i: beach your ship right there by deep-eddying Oceanus, and go yourself into the dank house of Hades.
sentences.n: νῆα … κέλσαι … ἰέναι are infinitives for imperatives, ‘beach the ship … and go’: κέλσαι is the aorist of κέλλω ‘run ashore’. αὐτοῦ is ‘on the spot, right there’, an adverb. βαθυδίνῃ is ‘deep-eddying’ (δίνη ‘eddy’), said of Ὠκεανῷ. Ἀίδεω is the genitive of Ἀΐδης with the uncontracted ending -εω, and εὐρώεντα is ‘mouldy, dank’, from εὐρώς ‘mould’: the epithet of the house of Hades.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν εἰς Ἀχέροντα Πυριφλεγέθων τε ῥέουσιν
Κώκυτός θ’, ὃς δὴ Στυγὸς ὕδατός ἐστιν ἀπορρώξ,
πέτρη τε ξύνεσίς τε δύω ποταμῶν ἐριδούπων·
sentences.tr:
entha men eis Acheronta Pyriphlegethōn te rheousin
Kōkytos th’, hos dē Stygos hydatos estin aporrōx,
petrē te xynesis te dyō potamōn eridoupōn·
sentences.i: There Pyriphlegethon flows into Acheron, and Cocytus too, which is an offshoot of the water of the Styx, and there is a rock and the meeting of two loud-echoing rivers;
sentences.n: ἔνθα μέν is ‘there’, and ῥέουσιν is the uncontracted ‘they flow’, with the two river-names Πυριφλεγέθων ‘fire-blazing’ (πῦρ + φλέγω) and Κώκυτος (apparently from κωκύω ‘wail’) as its subject, and εἰς Ἀχέροντα ‘into Acheron’. ὃς δὴ Στυγὸς ὕδατός ἐστιν ἀπορρώξ is ‘which is an offshoot of the water of the Styx’: ἀπορρώξ is something broken off, a branch. πέτρη τε ξύνεσίς τε is ‘both a rock and a meeting’, δύω is ‘two’, and ἐριδούπων is ‘loud-echoing’ (ἐρι- intensive + δοῦπος ‘din’).

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειθ’, ἥρως, χριμφθεὶς πέλας, ὥς σε κελεύω,
βόθρον ὀρύξαι, ὅσον τε πυγούσιον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα,
sentences.tr:
entha d’ epeith’, hērōs, chrimphtheis pelas, hōs se keleuō,
bothron oryxai, hoson te pygousion entha kai entha,
sentences.l:
There then, hero, having come close, as I bid you,
dig a pit, as much as a cubit’s length this way and that,
sentences.i: There, hero, when you have come close, as I bid you, dig a pit a cubit long in each direction,
sentences.n: ἥρως is ‘hero’ as a respectful address. χριμφθείς is the aorist passive participle of χρίμπτω ‘come near’, and ὥς σε κελεύω is ‘as I bid you’. βόθρον ὀρύξαι is an infinitive for an imperative, ‘dig a pit’. ὅσον τε πυγούσιον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα is ‘as much as a cubit this way and that’: πυγούσιον is a cubit's length (πυγών is the forearm), so the pit is a cubit across each way. The sentence is cut at this comma.

sentences.t:
ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ δὲ χοὴν χεῖσθαι πᾶσιν νεκύεσσιν,
πρῶτα μελικρήτῳ, μετέπειτα δὲ ἡδέι οἴνῳ,
τὸ τρίτον αὖθ’ ὕδατι· ἐπὶ δ’ ἄλφιτα λευκὰ παλύνειν.
sentences.tr:
amph’ autōi de choēn cheisthai pasin nekyessin,
prōta melikrētōi, metepeita de hēdei oinōi,
to triton auth’ hydati· epi d’ alphita leuka palynein.
sentences.l:
and around it pour a libation to all the dead,
first with honey-mixture, and after that with sweet wine,
the third time again with water; and over it sprinkle white barley-meal.
sentences.i: and around it pour a libation to all the dead, first of a honeyed mixture, then of sweet wine, and the third time of water; and sprinkle white barley-meal over it.
sentences.n: ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ is ‘around it’, the pit. χοήν is a poured offering (χέω ‘pour’), and χεῖσθαι is the infinitive for an imperative; πᾶσιν νεκύεσσιν is ‘to all the dead’, with the dative ending -εσσιν. πρῶτα … μετέπειτα … τὸ τρίτον are ‘first … next … the third time’. μελικρήτῳ is a mixture of honey (μέλι) and another liquid, traditionally milk. ἐπὶ … παλύνειν is tmesis, ‘sprinkle over’, and ἄλφιτα λευκά is ‘white barley-meal’.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ γουνοῦσθαι νεκύων ἀμενηνὰ κάρηνα,
ἐλθὼν εἰς Ἰθάκην στεῖραν βοῦν, ἥ τις ἀρίστη,
ῥέξειν ἐν μεγάροισι πυρήν τ’ ἐμπλησέμεν ἐσθλῶν,
sentences.tr:
polla de gounousthai nekyōn amenēna karēna,
elthōn eis Ithakēn steiran boun, hē tis aristē,
rhexein en megaroisi pyrēn t’ emplēsemen esthlōn,
sentences.l:
and much to entreat the powerless heads of the dead,
(promising that) when you have come to Ithaca, a barren cow, whichever is best,
you will sacrifice in your halls, and will fill a pyre with good things,
sentences.i: and entreat the powerless heads of the dead many times over, promising that when you reach Ithaca you will sacrifice in your halls a barren cow, the best you have, and fill a pyre with good things,
sentences.n: γουνοῦσθαι is ‘to entreat at the knees’ (γόνυ ‘knee’), another infinitive for an imperative. νεκύων ἀμενηνὰ κάρηνα is ‘the powerless heads of the dead’: ἀμενηνός is ‘without μένος, strength’, and κάρηνα, ‘heads’, stands for the persons. ῥέξειν and ἐμπλησέμεν (and ἱερευσέμεν in 524) are future infinitives giving the promise, ‘that you will sacrifice, and fill’. στεῖραν βοῦν is ‘a barren cow’, ἥ τις ἀρίστη ‘whichever is best’, and πυρὴν … ἐσθλῶν ‘a pyre with good things’ (genitive after ἐμπλησέμεν).

sentences.t:
Τειρεσίῃ δ’ ἀπάνευθεν ὄιν ἱερευσέμεν οἴῳ
παμμέλαν’, ὃς μήλοισι μεταπρέπει ὑμετέροισιν.
sentences.tr:
Teiresiēi d’ apaneuthen oin hiereusemen oiōi
pammelan’, hos mēloisi metaprepei hymeteroisin.
sentences.l:
and to Tiresias, apart, a sheep you will sacrifice, to him alone,
all-black, which among your flocks stands out.
sentences.i: and, apart from the rest, you will sacrifice to Tiresias alone a sheep, all black, the one that stands out among your flocks.
sentences.n: Τειρεσίῃ is the dative ‘to Tiresias’, and οἴῳ ‘alone’ agrees with it. ἀπάνευθεν is ‘apart’, ὄιν is ‘a sheep’ (ὄις), and ἱερευσέμεν is the future infinitive ‘to sacrifice’, continuing the promise. παμμέλαν’ is παμμέλανα ‘all-black’. ὃς μήλοισι μεταπρέπει ὑμετέροισιν is ‘which stands out among your flocks’: μεταπρέπω ‘be conspicuous among’, μῆλα ‘flocks’, ὑμετέροισιν ‘yours’, plural.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν εὐχῇσι λίσῃ κλυτὰ ἔθνεα νεκρῶν,
ἔνθ’ ὄιν ἀρνειὸν ῥέζειν θῆλύν τε μέλαιναν
εἰς Ἔρεβος στρέψας, αὐτὸς δ’ ἀπονόσφι τραπέσθαι
ἱέμενος ποταμοῖο ῥοάων·
sentences.tr:
autar epēn euchēisi lisēi klyta ethnea nekrōn,
enth’ oin arneion rhezein thēlyn te melainan
eis Erebos strepsas, autos d’ aponosphi trapesthai
hiemenos potamoio rhoaōn·
sentences.l:
But when with prayers you have besought the famous tribes of the dead,
then a sheep, a ram, sacrifice, and a female, black,
having turned them toward Erebus, and yourself turn away,
making for the streams of the river;
sentences.i: But when you have besought the famous tribes of the dead with your prayers, sacrifice a ram and a black ewe, turning them toward Erebus, and turn yourself away, making for the river’s streams;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπήν is ‘but when’ (= ἐπεάν), with λίσῃ the aorist subjunctive of λίσσομαι ‘beseech’ and εὐχῇσι ‘with prayers’. κλυτὰ ἔθνεα νεκρῶν is ‘the famous tribes of the dead’ (ἔθνος is a body of people or beings). ὄιν ἀρνειόν is ‘a sheep, a ram’, and ῥέζειν ‘sacrifice’, an infinitive for an imperative. εἰς Ἔρεβος στρέψας is ‘having turned them toward Erebus’, the dark place of the dead. ἀπονόσφι τραπέσθαι is ‘turn away’, and ἱέμενος ποταμοῖο ῥοάων ‘making for the river's streams’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ πολλαὶ
ψυχαὶ ἐλεύσονται νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων.
sentences.tr:
entha de pollai
psychai eleusontai nekyōn katatethnēōtōn.
sentences.l:
and there many
souls will come of the dead, of those who have died.
sentences.i: and there many souls of those who have died will come.
sentences.n: ἔνθα δέ is ‘and there’. ψυχαί is ‘souls’: the ψυχή is the life-breath that leaves the body at death, as when Elpenor's ψυχή goes down to Hades (560). νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων is ‘of the dead, of those who have died’: κατατεθνηώτων is the uncontracted genitive plural of the perfect participle of καταθνήσκω, and ἐλεύσονται is the future ‘will come’. The unit starts in the middle of line 529.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότ’ ἔπειθ’ ἑτάροισιν ἐποτρῦναι καὶ ἀνῶξαι
μῆλα, τὰ δὴ κατάκειτ’ ἐσφαγμένα νηλέι χαλκῷ,
δείραντας κατακῆαι, ἐπεύξασθαι δὲ θεοῖσιν,
ἰφθίμῳ τ’ Ἀίδῃ καὶ ἐπαινῇ Περσεφονείῃ·
sentences.tr:
dē tot’ epeith’ hetaroisin epotrynai kai anōxai
mēla, ta dē katakeit’ esphagmena nēlei chalkōi,
deirantas katakēai, epeuxasthai de theoisin,
iphthimōi t’ Aidēi kai epainēi Persephoneiēi·
sentences.l:
Then at that time next to your companions to urge on and to command
the sheep which lie slain by pitiless bronze,
having flayed them, to burn them, and to pray to the gods,
to mighty Hades and to grim Persephone;
sentences.i: Then, at that point, urge your companions on and order them to flay the sheep that lie there slain by the pitiless bronze, and to burn them, and to pray to the gods, to mighty Hades and grim Persephone;
sentences.n: ἑταίροισιν ἐποτρῦναι καὶ ἀνῶξαι is ‘to urge on and to order your companions’, both infinitives standing for imperatives, with μῆλα, ‘the sheep’, as what they are to deal with. κατάκειτ’ ἐσφαγμένα is ‘lie slain’ (ἐσφαγμένα, the perfect passive participle of σφάζω), νηλέι χαλκῷ ‘by pitiless bronze’. δείραντας κατακῆαι is ‘having flayed, to burn’, and ἐπεύξασθαι ‘to pray’ takes the dative θεοῖσιν. ἰφθίμῳ Ἀίδῃ is ‘mighty Hades’ and ἐπαινῇ Περσεφονείῃ ‘grim Persephone’, in the dative.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δὲ ξίφος ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ
ἧσθαι, μηδὲ ἐᾶν νεκύων ἀμενηνὰ κάρηνα
αἵματος ἆσσον ἴμεν, πρὶν Τειρεσίαο πυθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
autos de xiphos oxy eryssamenos para mērou
hēsthai, mēde ean nekyōn amenēna karēna
haimatos asson imen, prin Teiresiao pythesthai.
sentences.l:
and yourself, a sharp sword having drawn from beside your thigh,
sit, and do not allow the powerless heads of the dead
nearer the blood to go, before of Tiresias you have inquired.
sentences.i: And you yourself, drawing your sharp sword from beside your thigh, sit there, and do not let the powerless heads of the dead come nearer the blood until you have inquired of Tiresias.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς δέ is ‘and you yourself’, turning from the companions to Odysseus. ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, and ξίφος ὀξύ is ‘a sharp sword’. ἧσθαι ‘to sit’ is again an infinitive for an imperative. μηδὲ ἐᾶν … ἴμεν is ‘and do not allow … to go’ (ἴμεν is the epic infinitive of εἶμι), and αἵματος ἆσσον is ‘nearer the blood’. πρὶν Τειρεσίαο πυθέσθαι is ‘before you have inquired of Tiresias’, with the genitive of the person asked.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα τοι αὐτίκα μάντις ἐλεύσεται, ὄρχαμε λαῶν,
ὅς κέν τοι εἴπῃσιν ὁδὸν καὶ μέτρα κελεύθου
νόστον θ’, ὡς ἐπὶ πόντον ἐλεύσεαι ἰχθυόεντα.
sentences.tr:
entha toi autika mantis eleusetai, orchame laōn,
hos ken toi eipēisin hodon kai metra keleuthou
noston th’, hōs epi ponton eleuseai ichthyoenta.
sentences.l:
There to you at once a seer will come, chief of the people,
who would tell you the way and the measures of your path
and of your return, how you shall come upon the fish-teeming sea.’
sentences.i: There the seer will come to you at once, chief of the people, and he will tell you the way and the distances of your journey, and how you are to make your way home across the fish-teeming sea.’
sentences.n: ἔνθα τοι αὐτίκα μάντις ἐλεύσεται is ‘there to you at once a seer will come’. ὄρχαμε λαῶν is the vocative ‘chief of the people’. ὅς κέν τοι εἴπῃσιν is ‘who will tell you’, with κεν and the aorist subjunctive. μέτρα κελεύθου is ‘the measures of your path’, the stages and distances. νόστον … ὡς … ἐλεύσεαι is ‘your return, how you will come’, with ἰχθυόεντα ‘fish-teeming’. Lines 539–540 are a shipped formula and their English is kept. Circe's speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτίκα δὲ χρυσόθρονος ἤλυθεν Ἠώς.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autika de chrysothronos ēlythen Ēōs.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and at once golden-throned Dawn came.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and golden-throned Dawn came at once.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so she spoke’, and αὐτίκα δέ ‘and at once’. χρυσόθρονος Ἠώς is ‘golden-throned Dawn’, with an epithet from θρόνος ‘seat’; an old alternative derives the second part from θρόνα ‘embroidered flowers’. ἤλυθεν is the epic aorist ‘came’, the same as ἦλθεν.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δέ με χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα ἕσσεν·
sentences.tr: amphi de me chlainan te chitōna te heimata hessen·
sentences.l: and about me both a cloak and a tunic, as clothing, she put on me;
sentences.i: and she put clothes about me, a cloak and a tunic;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δέ με … ἕσσεν is ‘and about me she put’: ἀμφί stands apart from the verb (tmesis), and ἕσσεν is the aorist of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, with με ‘me’ as its object. εἵματα ‘clothes’ is then spelled out as χλαῖναν ‘a cloak’ and χιτῶνα ‘a tunic’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ δ’ ἀργύφεον φᾶρος μέγα ἕννυτο νύμφη,
λεπτὸν καὶ χαρίεν, περὶ δὲ ζώνην βάλετ’ ἰξυῖ
καλὴν χρυσείην, κεφαλῇ δ’ ἐπέθηκε καλύπτρην.
sentences.tr:
autē d’ argypheon pharos mega hennyto nymphē,
lepton kai charien, peri de zōnēn balet’ ixui
kalēn chryseiēn, kephalēi d’ epethēke kalyptrēn.
sentences.l:
and she herself, the nymph, put on a great silver-white robe,
fine and graceful, and around her waist she threw a girdle,
fair, golden, and on her head she set a veil.
sentences.i: and the nymph herself put on a great silver-white robe, fine and graceful, threw a fair golden girdle about her waist, and set a veil upon her head.
sentences.n: αὐτὴ δ’ … ἕννυτο is ‘and she herself put on’, the imperfect middle of ἕννυμι. ἀργύφεον is ‘silver-white’, φᾶρος ‘robe’, and λεπτὸν καὶ χαρίεν ‘fine and graceful’. περὶ … βάλετο is tmesis, ‘threw around’, and ἰξυῖ is the dative ‘about the waist’; ζώνην … καλὴν χρυσείην is ‘a fair golden girdle’. καλύπτρη is ‘veil’. Lines 543–544 are shipped, and 545 differs from the published line only in ἐπέθηκε ‘set upon’ for ἐφύπερθε.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ διὰ δώματ’ ἰὼν ὤτρυνον ἑταίρους
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι παρασταδὸν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον·
sentences.tr:
autar egō dia dōmat’ iōn ōtrynon hetairous
meilichiois epeessi parastadon andra hekaston·
sentences.l:
But I, going through the house, urged on my companions
with gentle words, standing-beside each man:
sentences.i: But I went through the house and urged my companions on with gentle words, standing beside each man:
sentences.n: διὰ δώματ’ ἰών is ‘going through the house’: δώματα is a plural for one house. ὤτρυνον is the imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι is ‘with gentle words’, the dative plurals of μειλίχιος and ἔπος, and παρασταδόν is ‘standing beside’, an adverb, with ἄνδρα ἕκαστον ‘each man’. The second line is a shipped formula and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
μηκέτι νῦν εὕδοντες ἀωτεῖτε γλυκὺν ὕπνον,
ἀλλ’ ἴομεν·
sentences.tr:
mēketi nyn heudontes aōteite glykyn hypnon,
all’ iomen·
sentences.l:
‘No longer now sleeping slumber sweet sleep,
but let us go;
sentences.i: ‘No longer lie asleep now, slumbering in sweet sleep, but let us go;
sentences.n: μηκέτι νῦν is ‘no longer now’, with εὕδοντες ‘sleeping’ and ἀωτεῖτε, a rare plural imperative: it is taken to mean ‘sleep, slumber’, but its formation is not certain. γλυκὺν ὕπνον is ‘sweet sleep’, the internal accusative. ἀλλ’ ἴομεν is ‘but let us go’: ἴομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive of εἶμι (Attic ἴωμεν). The unit ends at the raised point inside line 549.

sentences.t: δὴ γάρ μοι ἐπέφραδε πότνια Κίρκη.
sentences.tr: dē gar moi epephrade potnia Kirkē.
sentences.l: for indeed to me has pointed out the lady Circe.’
sentences.i: for the lady Circe has already told me.’
sentences.n: δὴ γάρ is ‘for indeed, for already’. ἐπέφραδε is the aorist of ἐπιφράζω ‘point out, tell’, and μοι is ‘to me’. πότνια Κίρκη is ‘the lady Circe’: πότνια ‘lady, mistress’ is a title of goddesses. The unit begins in the middle of line 549, and the speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, toisin d’ epepeitheto thymos agēnōr.
sentences.l: So I spoke, and in them their manly spirit was persuaded.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and their proud spirits were won over.
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’. τοῖσιν is ‘in them’, a pronoun with the epic dative ending -σιν. ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is the phrase of 475, now said of the men: the singular θυμός stands for the spirit of each of them.

sentences.t: οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδ’ ἔνθεν περ ἀπήμονας ἦγον ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr: oude men oud’ enthen per apēmonas ēgon hetairous.
sentences.l: But not even from there, indeed, unharmed did I lead my companions.
sentences.i: But not even from there did I bring my companions away unharmed.
sentences.n: οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδ’ … περ is an emphatic ‘but not even’, and ἔνθεν is ‘from there’ (the suffix -θεν marks the place from which). ἀπήμονας is ‘unharmed’ (ἀ- + πῆμα ‘woe, harm’), agreeing with ἑταίρους, and ἦγον is the imperfect ‘I was leading’.

sentences.t:
Ἐλπήνωρ δέ τις ἔσκε νεώτατος, οὔτε τι λίην
ἄλκιμος ἐν πολέμῳ οὔτε φρεσὶν ᾗσιν ἀρηρώς·
sentences.tr:
Elpēnōr de tis eske neōtatos, oute ti liēn
alkimos en polemōi oute phresin hēisin arērōs·
sentences.l:
And a certain Elpenor there was, the youngest,
not very much valiant in war nor sound in his own wits;
sentences.i: There was a certain Elpenor, the youngest, not very valiant in war and not sound in his own wits;
sentences.n: Ἐλπήνωρ δέ τις ἔσκε is ‘and there was a certain Elpenor’: ἔσκε is an iterative form of εἰμί, here simply ‘was’, and νεώτατος is ‘youngest’. οὔτε τι λίην ἄλκιμος is ‘not very valiant’ (λίην ‘very’). φρεσὶν ᾗσιν ἀρηρώς is ‘sound in his own wits’: ἀρηρώς is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit, fix’, and ᾗσιν is the possessive ‘his own’, not a relative. The same words come again in 557.

sentences.t:
ὅς μοι ἄνευθ’ ἑτάρων ἱεροῖς ἐν δώμασι Κίρκης,
ψύχεος ἱμείρων, κατελέξατο οἰνοβαρείων.
sentences.tr:
hos moi aneuth’ hetarōn hierois en dōmasi Kirkēs,
psycheos himeirōn, katelexato oinobareiōn.
sentences.l:
who for me, apart from his companions, in the sacred house of Circe,
longing for coolness, lay down, heavy with wine.
sentences.i: who, apart from his companions, in Circe’s sacred house, longing for the cool air, had lain down heavy with wine.
sentences.n: ὅς μοι is ‘who, of mine’, a relative with a dative of interest. ἄνευθ’ ἑτάρων is ‘apart from his companions’, and ἱεροῖς ἐν δώμασι Κίρκης ‘in the sacred house of Circe’ (δώμασι plural for one house). ψύχεος ἱμείρων is ‘longing for coolness’: ψῦχος takes the genitive after ἱμείρω ‘long for’. κατελέξατο is ‘laid himself down’, the aorist middle of καταλέγω, and οἰνοβαρείων ‘weighed down with wine’ is a rare participle from οἶνος and βαρύς ‘heavy’.

sentences.t:
κινυμένων δ’ ἑτάρων ὅμαδον καὶ δοῦπον ἀκούσας
ἐξαπίνης ἀνόρουσε καὶ ἐκλάθετο φρεσὶν ᾗσιν
ἄψορρον καταβῆναι ἰὼν ἐς κλίμακα μακρήν,
ἀλλὰ καταντικρὺ τέγεος πέσεν·
sentences.tr:
kinymenōn d’ hetarōn homadon kai doupon akousas
exapinēs anorouse kai eklatheto phresin hēisin
apsorron katabēnai iōn es klimaka makrēn,
alla katantikry tegeos pesen·
sentences.l:
of his companions stirring, the din and the clatter hearing,
suddenly he leapt up, and forgot in his own wits
to go back down, going to the long ladder,
but straight down from the roof he fell;
sentences.i: As soon as he heard the din and the clatter of his companions stirring, he suddenly leapt up, and in his own wits forgot to go back down, making for the long ladder, but fell straight down from the roof;
sentences.n: κινυμένων … ἑτάρων is the genitive plural of the participle of κινύομαι ‘move, stir’, ‘of his companions stirring’, which depends on ὅμαδον ‘din’ and δοῦπον ‘clatter’, the sounds he heard. ἐξαπίνης is ‘suddenly’, and ἀνόρουσε ‘he leapt up’ is unaugmented. ἐκλάθετο φρεσὶν ᾗσιν is ‘he forgot in his own wits’, with ᾗσιν the possessive again, followed by ἄψορρον καταβῆναι ‘to go back down’ and ἐς κλίμακα μακρήν ‘to the long ladder’. καταντικρὺ τέγεος πέσεν is ‘straight down from the roof he fell’: πέσεν is unaugmented, and τέγεος is the genitive of τέγος ‘roof’. Line 559 is metrically irregular as transmitted: καταντικρύ fits the hexameter only if its last syllable is lengthened, at the start of the third foot.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δέ οἱ αὐχὴν
ἀστραγάλων ἐάγη, ψυχὴ δ’ Ἄϊδόσδε κατῆλθεν.
sentences.tr:
ek de hoi auchēn
astragalōn eagē, psychē d’ Aïdosde katēlthen.
sentences.l:
and from him the neck
out of the vertebrae was broken, and his soul to Hades went down.
sentences.i: and his neck was broken away from the vertebrae, and his soul went down to Hades.
sentences.n: ἐκ δέ οἱ αὐχὴν ἀστραγάλων ἐάγη is ‘and from him the neck was broken out of the vertebrae’: ἐκ … ἐάγη is tmesis, the aorist passive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’; οἱ is ‘from him’, αὐχήν ‘neck’, and ἀστραγάλων the genitive of ἀστράγαλος, here the neck-bones (the word also means ‘knucklebone’). ψυχὴ δ’ Ἄϊδόσδε κατῆλθεν is ‘and his soul went down to Hades’: the suffix -δε marks direction, so Ἄϊδόσδε is ‘to Hades’. The unit begins in the middle of line 559.

sentences.t: ἐρχομένοισι δὲ τοῖσιν ἐγὼ μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπον·
sentences.tr: erchomenoisi de toisin egō meta mython eeipon·
sentences.l: And to them as they went, among them a speech I spoke:
sentences.i: And as they went on their way, I spoke among them:
sentences.n: ἐρχομένοισι … τοῖσιν is ‘to them as they went’, the dative plural participle with the pronoun. μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπον is ‘I spoke a speech among them’: μετά … ἔειπον is tmesis of μετεῖπον ‘speak among’, ἔειπον being the epic aorist of λέγω.

sentences.t:
φάσθε νύ που οἶκόνδε φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
ἔρχεσθ’·
sentences.tr:
phasthe ny pou oikonde philēn es patrida gaian
erchesth’·
sentences.l:
‘You suppose, then, I think, homeward to your dear fatherland
to be going;
sentences.i: ‘No doubt you suppose that you are going home to your dear fatherland;
sentences.n: φάσθε νύ που is ‘you suppose, no doubt’: φάσθε is the second plural of φημί (middle), ‘you think’, and it governs ἔρχεσθ’, the elided infinitive ἔρχεσθαι, ‘that you are going’. οἶκόνδε is ‘homeward’, with the suffix -δε of direction. φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘to your dear fatherland’, πατρίδα γαῖαν being a stock phrase. The next unit corrects what the men suppose.

sentences.t:
ἄλλην δ’ ἧμιν ὁδὸν τεκμήρατο Κίρκη,
εἰς Ἀίδαο δόμους καὶ ἐπαινῆς Περσεφονείης
ψυχῇ χρησομένους Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο.
sentences.tr:
allēn d’ hēmin hodon tekmērato Kirkē,
eis Aidao domous kai epainēs Persephoneiēs
psychēi chrēsomenous Thēbaiou Teiresiao.
sentences.l:
but another journey for us Circe has fixed,
to the halls of Hades and of grim Persephone,
to consult the soul of Theban Tiresias.’
sentences.i: but Circe has fixed another journey for us, to the halls of Hades and grim Persephone, to consult the soul of Theban Tiresias.’
sentences.n: ἄλλην δ’ ἧμιν ὁδὸν τεκμήρατο Κίρκη is ‘but another journey for us Circe has fixed’: ἧμιν is ἡμῖν ‘for us’, and τεκμήρατο is the aorist middle of τεκμαίρομαι ‘fix, ordain’. Lines 564–565 repeat 491–492 word for word, Circe's own words now in Odysseus' mouth, and their English is kept. The unit begins in the middle of line 563, and the speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, τοῖσιν δὲ κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ,
ἑζόμενοι δὲ κατ’ αὖθι γόων τίλλοντό τε χαίτας·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephamēn, toisin de kateklasthē philon ētor,
hezomenoi de kat’ authi goōn tillonto te chaitas·
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and in them was broken their dear heart,
and sitting down right there they wailed and tore their hair;
sentences.i: So I spoke, and their dear hearts were broken within them; and sitting down right there they wailed and tore at their hair;
sentences.n: The first line is the formula of 496 with the persons changed: τοῖσιν is ‘in them’, κατεκλάσθη the aorist passive ‘was broken’. ἑζόμενοι is the participle of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’, and κατ’ αὖθι is κατ’ αὐτόθι ‘right there’. γόων is the unaugmented imperfect ‘they wailed’ (3 pl. of γοάω), and τίλλοντο the imperfect middle of τίλλω ‘pluck, tear’; χαίτας is ‘hair’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ τις πρῆξις ἐγίγνετο μυρομένοισιν.
sentences.tr: all’ ou gar tis prēxis egigneto myromenoisin.
sentences.l: but not any accomplishing came about for them lamenting.
sentences.i: but nothing was accomplished by their lamenting.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ is ‘but (it did no good), for …’; the thought the Greek leaves out is that weeping was useless. πρῆξις is ‘accomplishing, getting something done’, ἐγίγνετο the imperfect of γίγνομαι ‘come about’, and μυρομένοισιν the dative plural participle of μύρομαι ‘lament’, ‘for them lamenting’. The line is shipped and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης
ᾔομεν ἀχνύμενοι θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντες,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ epi nēa thoēn kai thina thalassēs
ēiomen achnymenoi thaleron kata dakry cheontes,
sentences.l:
But when at last to the swift ship and the shore of the sea
we went, grieving, an abundant tear shedding down,
sentences.i: But when at last we were making our way to the swift ship and the shore of the sea, grieving and shedding abundant tears,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ῥ’ is ‘but when at last’ (ῥά = ἄρα). νῆα θοήν is ‘swift ship’, θοήν the stock epithet, and θῖνα θαλάσσης is ‘the shore of the sea’. ᾔομεν is the imperfect of εἶμι, ‘we were going’, and ἀχνύμενοι is ‘grieving’. θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντες is ‘shedding abundant tears’: κατὰ … χέοντες is tmesis, ‘pouring down’, and θαλερός, ‘blooming’, is here ‘abundant’. The sentence is cut at this comma.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δ’ ἄρ’ οἰχομένη Κίρκη παρὰ νηὶ μελαίνῃ
ἀρνειὸν κατέδησεν ὄιν θῆλύν τε μέλαιναν,
ῥεῖα παρεξελθοῦσα·
sentences.tr:
tophra d’ ar’ oichomenē Kirkē para nēi melainēi
arneion katedēsen oin thēlyn te melainan,
rheia parexelthousa·
sentences.i: Meanwhile Circe had gone off and, passing easily by, had tied a ram and a black ewe beside the black ship;
sentences.n: τόφρα δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and meanwhile’. οἰχομένη is ‘having gone off’ (οἴχομαι ‘be gone’), and κατέδησεν is the aorist of καταδέω ‘tie up’, with ἀρνειὸν … ὄιν θῆλύν τε μέλαιναν, ‘a ram, a sheep, and a black female’, the very victims she named at 527. ῥεῖα is ‘easily’, and παρεξελθοῦσα is the aorist participle ‘having gone past (us)’.

sentences.t:
τίς ἂν θεὸν οὐκ ἐθέλοντα
ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδοιτ’ ἢ ἔνθ’ ἢ ἔνθα κιόντα;
sentences.tr:
tis an theon ouk ethelonta
ophthalmoisin idoit’ ē enth’ ē entha kionta;
sentences.l:
who could a god not willing
with eyes see, either here or there going?
sentences.i: Who could see a god with his eyes against his will, as he goes this way or that?
sentences.n: τίς ἂν … ἴδοιτ’ is ‘who could see …?’: ἄν with the optative gives the potential, and ἴδοιτ’ is the elided middle form ἴδοιτο, the same sense as ἴδοι. It is a rhetorical question, Odysseus' own comment as narrator, and the answer is ‘no one’. θεὸν οὐκ ἐθέλοντα is ‘a god not willing’, ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ‘with the eyes’, and ἢ ἔνθ’ ἢ ἔνθα κιόντα ‘going either here or there’. The Greek question mark ends the unit.
